chunks: My father (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Sa'd ibn Abdillah narrated to me from Ya'qub ibn Yazid from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

Indeed, the last servant to be ordered to be taken to Hellfire will turn around and say. Allah, the Mighty and Sublime, will say: 'Hurry him.' When he is brought before Him, He will say to His servant: 'Why did you turn around?' He will say: 'O Lord, this was not my expectation of You.' Allah, Glory be to His Majesty, will say: 'My servant, and what was your expectation of Me?' He will say: 'O Lord, my expectation of You was that You would forgive my mistake and admit me into Your Paradise.'

Allah will say: 'My angels, My might, My majesty, My affliction, and the elevation of My status. Did this one expect anything good from Me for even a moment of his life?' He will say: 'If he had expected anything good from Me for even a moment of his life, I would not have terrified him with the Fire. Accept his lie and admit him into Paradise.'

Then Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'Whatever a servant expects of Allah as good, it will be for him according to that expectation.' And this is His, the Mighty and Sublime, saying: 'And that was your thought which you entertained about your Lord; it has brought you to ruin, so you have become of the lost ones.'

key_terms.أَجِیزُوا لَهُ کَذِبَهُ: Accept/validate his lie (his expectation of good)
key_terms.أَعْجِلُوهُ: Hurry him (to be brought before God)
key_terms.الْخاسِرِینَ: The lost ones (those who suffer loss in the Hereafter)
key_terms.ظَنّ: Expectation or assumption (about God's nature or decree)

ai.seo_question: How does a sinner's expectation of God determine their final destination in the afterlife?
ai.summary: This hadith from Shaykh al-Saduq’s *Thawab al-A'mal* elucidates the Shia doctrine of *Husn al-Zann* (good expectation) as a decisive factor in divine mercy, illustrating that God’s judgment is often aligned with the servant’s sincere hope rather than strict retribution. The narrative of the sinner being returned from Hellfire underscores the theological principle that God’s greatness is measured by His capacity to forgive, validating the servant's expectation as truth. This concept is deeply rooted in the Quranic maxim that God acts according to what His servants expect of Him, reinforcing the balance between justice and mercy in Shia jurisprudence and spirituality.
